btos.label: Real estate and rental and leasing (NAICS 53)

name: Real Estate
blurb: Automated valuation is the sector's oldest AI and now federally regulated under FHFA and CFPB quality-control rules; plus valuation, leasing, and property-management platforms with methodology disclosed.

points.desc: Census BTOS reports real-estate sector AI use directly from firms.
points.name: Adoption is measured, not guessed

points.desc: The interagency Quality Control Standards for Automated Valuation Models - finalized by FHFA, CFPB, and the banking regulators - are the first binding federal rules for the sector's core AI: the models that value homes in mortgage decisions.
points.name: AVMs are now federally regulated AI

points.desc: The bureau's AVM rule page and its algorithmic-appraisal work are the record of how valuation bias and model accountability are supervised.
points.name: CFPB carries the consumer-protection side

points.name: Zillow and Redfin publish their valuation models

points.name: Opendoor prices houses with models at risk

points.desc: JLL and CBRE - the commercial real estate services majors - deploy generative and predictive AI across brokerage, facilities, and portfolio analytics.
points.name: The CRE giants run enterprise AI

points.desc: 3D capture and computer vision digitizing physical space - the data layer under virtual touring and property intelligence.

points.name: Leasing and property ops are automating

points.name: CREtech and MetaProp track the proptech market

points.desc: The Building Owners and Managers Association tracks AI in smart-building operations, energy efficiency, and predictive maintenance across commercial property.
points.name: BOMA covers commercial building operations

points.desc: The realtor association's technology accelerator is where residential proptech gets vetted and scaled - a window into which tools the profession is actually adopting.
points.name: NAR REACH backs the startups

points.desc: The residential brokerage's platform applies AI to agent workflows, client matching, and predictive listing recommendations.
points.name: Compass runs AI inside the brokerage workflow

points.desc: HouseCanary's valuation and forecasting models and Cherre's data integration layer are what institutional investors underwrite on - the wholesale side of the AVM story.
points.name: Institutional valuation runs on data platforms

points.desc: Prophia extracts terms, rent rolls, and obligations from commercial leases automatically - one of the clearest production uses of document AI in the sector.
points.name: Lease abstraction is a document-AI problem

points.desc: Visitt and Building Engines apply IoT sensing and machine learning to HVAC optimization, maintenance prediction, and tenant workflow in operating buildings.
points.name: Smart buildings close the operations loop

summary: Automated valuation is the sector's oldest deployed AI, and it is now formally regulated: federal quality-control standards for AVMs took effect in 2025. Valuation, leasing automation, 3D capture, and property operations are where AI actually runs; the regulator record and the platforms' own model documentation are the sources.

analysis.body:
Per the Census Bureau's Business Trends and Outlook Survey, 28.0% of firms in real estate and rental and leasing reported using AI in the most recent period, up from 25.6% in the prior period, making it one of the more measurably active sectors in the survey. That headline figure spans a wide range of applications, from consumer-facing valuation tools to back-office document processing to building operations, and the sources collectively show that adoption is neither uniform nor new.

Automated valuation is the sector's longest-running and now most consequential AI deployment. Zillow publishes Zestimate home valuations for more than 110 million homes using a neural network-based model that draws on county and tax assessor records, MLS feeds, and listing signals, with updates running multiple times per week. HouseCanary offers AI-powered valuations, forecasts, and analytics covering more than 136 million U.S. properties, combining machine learning algorithms with image recognition that identifies room types and assesses home condition from photos. Opendoor applies similar models directly to purchasing decisions, carrying the pricing risk on its own balance sheet across more than 307,155 homeowners served. The regulatory environment around these models has hardened considerably: the CFPB, FHFA, OCC, Federal Reserve, FDIC, and NCUA jointly finalized quality control standards for automated valuation models used by mortgage originators and secondary market issuers, requiring institutions to adopt policies ensuring high confidence in estimates, protection against data manipulation, conflict-of-interest controls, and random sample testing and reviews.

In commercial real estate, AI is moving into operations and document management alongside valuation. Prophia uses AI to extract key lease terms from commercial lease documents and combines that extraction with expert validation to produce structured data on rent rolls, obligations, and risk exposure. Building Engines, a JLL company, positions its Prism platform as an AI-powered property management system that standardizes portfolio data, surfaces performance dashboards, and delivers recommendations aimed at improving net operating income. JLL states it has invested more in AI technology than any other real estate company, deploying it across brokerage, facilities, and portfolio analytics. Matterport digitizes physical buildings into 3D models that support virtual tours, floor plan generation, and portfolio management decisions, and integrates with Procore and Autodesk for construction workflows.

On the residential brokerage and leasing side, AI is being embedded into agent workflows and tenant communications. Compass applies AI within its brokerage platform to support agent productivity, client matching, and listing recommendations, while also offering a Concierge program that covers the cost of home improvement services ahead of sale. EliseAI operates as an agentic conversational AI platform for property management, handling inbound leads, scheduling tours, answering questions, and processing maintenance requests around the clock without human intervention. The National Association of Realtors tracks technology adoption across the profession, and its REACH accelerator, run through Second Century Ventures, functions as a vetting and scaling channel for residential proptech tools. CREtech, which convenes more than 3,000 leaders at its annual conference, and the Center for Real Estate Technology and Innovation serve as the commercial sector's primary networks for tracking where capital and strategy are concentrating.

The regulatory picture is the most concrete risk signal in the data. The interagency AVM final rule is the first binding federal framework specifically targeting an AI system central to real estate, and it applies to any institution making credit decisions or securitization determinations using such models. Compliance requires formal governance structures, not just technical accuracy. For operators considering AI deployment, the practical implication is that valuation models touching mortgage collateral now carry explicit regulatory obligations, while leasing automation and building operations tools remain less constrained but are not without fair housing and consumer protection considerations that the CFPB and BOMA both monitor. Organizations deciding whether to deploy should account for the fact that the most mature and documented AI applications in the sector, the consumer AVM platforms, took nearly two decades of continuous refinement to reach current accuracy levels, suggesting that newer deployments in lease abstraction and operational analytics will require sustained investment in data quality and human validation before they can be relied on at scale.
